title: Ferry Fare Change
story: You run the ticket window for a river ferry. A crossing costs $5, and each passenger pays with one $5, $10 or $20 bill. Your cash box starts empty, so the only change you can give is bills earlier passengers paid with. You know today's queue in advance and want to find out whether everyone can be served.
task: Write canGiveChange(bills). bills[i] is the bill the i-th passenger pays with, in queue order. Each passenger buys exactly one $5 ticket. Return true if you can give every passenger correct change, and false as soon as one passenger cannot get it.
Bills you receive go into the cash box and can be used as change for later passengers. An empty queue returns true.

examples.explanation: After two exact payments the box holds two $5. The $10 passenger gets a $5 back, leaving one $5 and one $10. The $20 passenger needs $15, so you give back the $10 and the $5.
After two passengers the box holds one $10 and no $5. The third passenger needs $5 back, and a $10 bill cannot be split.

hints: A $5 and a $10 are not equally useful as change. Think about which passengers a $10 can help and which ones need a $5.
A $10 passenger needs $5 back. A $20 passenger needs $15, which you can give as $10 + $5 or as $5 + $5 + $5. The $10 is only useful in the first combination.
When a $20 arrives and either combination works, consider which choice leaves more $5 bills for later passengers.

Count the $5 and $10 bills in the box, since a $20 is never useful as change. For a $10 payment, give back a $5. For a $20 payment, prefer $10 + $5 and use three $5s only when there is no $10. Return false as soon as a payment cannot be handled.
bruteForce: Each $20 passenger can get change up to two ways. Trying both options for each of them means up to 2k sequences for k such passengers, which is about a trillion for 40. Most of that work is wasted, because one choice is never worse than the other.

js: * @return {boolean} true if every passenger gets exact change

tests.note: paying 20 with three 5s first fails later
long queue, fails near the end

js: let fives = 0, tens = 0; // $20 bills are never given as change
tens--; fives--; // spend the less useful $10 first
py: fives = tens = 0  # $20 bills are never given as change
tens -= 1  # spend the less useful $10 first
walkthrough: A $5 can help any future passenger, while a $10 only helps a $20 passenger. When you have a choice, spend the less flexible bill and keep the $5s.
The trace below uses [5, 5, 5, 5, 10, 20, 10] and tracks the counts as (fives, tens).
• The four $5 passengers leave the box at (4, 0).
• The $20 passenger gets a $10 and a $5 back, not three $5s, giving (2, 0).
• The last $10 passenger gets a $5 back, giving (1, 1). Everyone has been served, so the answer is true.
Paying the $20 with three $5s would leave (0, 1), and the last passenger could not get their $5 back. The total amount of money would be the same, but the bills would be the wrong ones.
solution.timeWhy: One pass over the queue, constant work per passenger.
solution.takeaway: When two choices meet today's need equally well, pick the one that keeps the most options open for later. Here that means spending the bill that can serve fewer future cases.
